The cake-intermediate blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous or virus-retention membranes. It predicts permeate volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure rise over time during constant-flow operation. The model combines loss of available membrane area through intermediate blocking with increasing flow resistance from cake formation, using Darcy’s law to derive explicit time-dependent equations. The authors evaluated it with human plasma IgG filtered through Durapore PVDF membranes and BSA filtered through Viresolve 180

The combined cake-standard blocking model describes fouling of a membrane by both cake formation on its surface and pore constriction within the membrane. It predicts filtered volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure over time during constant-flow operation, using Darcy’s law and the two mechanisms’ effects on filtration resistance. The model has two fitted parameters and is formulated with algebraic relations rather than dynamic state equations. The Complete-standard blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous membranes by combining complete pore blockage with standard blocking, in which deposits constrict pores. It predicts permeate volume over time at constant pressure and pressure over time at constant flow, using explicit relationships derived from Darcy’s law. The model has two fitted fouling parameters and is intended for cases where both mechanisms are relevant; it reduces to the corresponding single-mechanism model when one mechanism dominates. The model describes protein fouling during microfiltration of bovine serum albumin solutions through polycarbonate membranes. It predicts how filtrate flow and flux decline over time as protein aggregates first cover open membrane areas and a protein deposit then grows over the covered regions. The full model combines flow through uncovered and covered areas and accounts for differences in deposit resistance according to when each region was first covered; the authors also derive a simpler approximate solution.
